The gestation period leading to this birth, observed under controlled aquarium conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C], lasts roughly 274.5 days [ab = roughly 274.5 days], a duration that reflects the protracted yolk-dependent embryonic development typical of many rajiform skates. This comparatively long embryonic phase allows for the differentiation of the complex morphological structures, including the distinct dorsal spots that give the species its common name, before the neonate is fully formed and ready to hatch. The allocation of maternal resources into a relatively small number of large, well-developed offspring is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes juvenile survivorship over high fecundity, a pattern commonly observed in other members of the family Rajidae.

Females of this species reach a considerably larger maximum size than their male counterparts, with the ultimate total length documented at 132 centimeters [Li = 132 centimeters], a size that is among the largest recorded within the genus Atlantoraja and reflects the selective pressures on female fecundity. This dimorphism is likely driven by the selective pressures associated with fecundity, as larger female elasmobranchs can accommodate a greater number of developing embryos within their uteri. The contrast between the substantial adult body mass and the moderate annual reproductive rate highlights a conservative life-history tactic.

Such a delayed onset of gonad maturation suggests that individuals must invest several years in somatic growth before allocating resources toward the production of offspring.

The maximum longevity for the spotback skate has been estimated at roughly 9855 days [am = roughly 9855 days] under a thermal regime of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C], marking it as a relatively long-lived species among its congeners. This extended lifespan, combined with the delayed sexual maturation, results in a life cycle where a mature individual may have many years of reproductive opportunity ahead of it after finally reaching adulthood. The combination of a considerable ultimate body length achieved by females and an extended period of somatic growth before the first pupping event contributes to a generation time that is substantial relative to many teleost fishes occupying similar benthic niches. The relationship between body size and longevity is consistent with the broader metabolic theory of ecology, which predicts that larger, slower-growing organisms typically experience longer lifespans and lower annual mortality rates. These demographic characteristics make the spotback skate particularly vulnerable to overexploitation, as populations cannot quickly recover from sustained fishing pressure.

The conservative life-history parameters of the spotback skate have direct implications for population resilience and management. A modest annual reproductive output — roughly 20 pups per year from one litter per year — means that even moderate increases in adult mortality can lead to rapid population declines. Furthermore, the requirement for a thermally stable environment near 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C] for optimal embryonic development and juvenile growth may restrict the species to specific depth ranges and latitudes along the continental shelf of South America. The substantial body mass of mature females, reaching up to 20,700 grams [Wwi = up to 20,700 grams], also makes them a frequent target of both commercial and artisanal fisheries, where they are often taken as bycatch.
